messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nadim is a 56-year-old Middle Eastern American man who works as a social media manager and lives with his wife. When he speaks about the night that now divides his life into before and after, he does not tell it in a smooth sequence. He reaches a point and then stops, as if something clamps down inside him. Even in session he seems to approach the memory, recoil from it, and move away before it is complete.

The incident happened after work, when he was driving home and was pulled over by police. What stands out in the fragments he can bear to describe is how quickly the encounter turned physical and how little sense it made to him while it was happening. He remembers the metallic taste in his mouth with unusual force, as if the memory carries it intact into the present. When it comes back, he can taste it again so clearly that it seems to erase the room he is actually in. He recalls being shouted at, forced down, and feeling trapped inside a situation that was already out of control before he understood what he needed to do. What is hardest for him to live with is not only the officers’ violence but his own actions in those seconds. He had always thought of himself as measured and principled, someone who would respond with dignity. Instead, under pressure and fear, he reacted in ways that he feels went against who he is. He does not elaborate much, but he has come to believe that he failed some private moral test that night.

In the weeks afterward, Nadim found that strong emotion of any kind became something to avoid. Fear was there, but so were anger, shame, and bursts of horror that seemed to arrive without warning. He also began to pull back from things that might stir positive feelings. He stopped watching films with his wife if they were suspenseful or emotionally intense, then stopped watching most television altogether. News clips, police dramas, viral videos, even reading about public confrontations online became intolerable. Given that his job requires him to spend much of the day online, this became particularly difficult. He started skimming content in a narrow, mechanical way, clicking away from posts that referenced arrests, violence, or confrontation. Colleagues noticed that he was less willing to take on campaigns tied to current events. He did not explain much. He only knew that once an image or headline caught him, the taste would come back, followed by a surge of rage so strong it frightened him.

His daily life narrowed around vigilance. Entering any restaurant, office, or public venue, he first located the exits. He could not settle into a chair or conversation until he had mapped at least one way out, preferably two. He scanned faces, doorways, body movements, hands. If someone stood too close behind him in line or blocked part of a path, his body tightened before he could think. Even at home with his wife, in a place he knew was safe, he found himself unable to relax. He would check locks, look out windows, and monitor noises in the hallway or street. The effort of appearing normal exhausted him.

Over time he came to see these reactions not as excessive but as proof that he had learned something essential. He was certain the world was dangerous in a more fundamental way than he had once allowed himself to admit. He had also become convinced that people are not what they seem. A routine interaction could conceal humiliation or threat; an official face could shift without warning into something cruel. These beliefs entered ordinary moments. In work meetings he watched for changes in tone and posture rather than listening fully. In public he studied strangers for signs of volatility. The strain affected his marriage. His wife wanted him to go out more, to visit friends, to watch a movie together and have some version of their old evenings back, but Nadim often refused or sat through an outing visibly tense, preoccupied with the nearest door.

What finally brought him to seek help was the accumulation of these restrictions and the fear of what he was becoming. He had recently been triggered by work content he could not avoid, and the memory came in with the old taste and the same violent rush of anger before he shoved it away. He was shaken not only by the memory but by how incomplete it remained, how he still could not let himself know all of it. He came to treatment wanting relief, though even that desire is guarded. What frightens him most is that he may never feel safe again, and that if he lets the memory come fully, he will be overwhelmed by rage and by what it says about the world, about other people, and about himself.
